title: NASA Astronaut Discusses Life In Space With Fox News – December 15, 2025 (iss073m263361553)
description: Aboard the International Space Station, NASA astronaut Chris Williams discussed life and work aboard the orbital outpost during an in-flight interview Dec. 2 with Shannon Bream’s Sunday News Show on Fox News. Williams who arrived to the space station on Nov. 27 for his first flight, is in the midst of a long-duration mission aboard the microgravity laboratory to advance scientific knowledge and demonstrate new technologies for future human and robotic exploration flights as part of NASA’s Moon and Mars exploration approach, including lunar missions through NASA’s Artemis program.

Thank you so much.

OK, Chris, I want to start here.
What in the world is it like?
What are the emotions when you get the notification you

No less.
Yeah, it was a roller coaster of emotions.
I mean, this has been something that I've dreamed about ever
since I was a little kid and worked towards my whole life.
And it's not something I ever thought I'd have the chance to do.
It's really a huge responsibility.
We have this wonderful laboratory up here
and being entrusted to help take care and push forward
the sides that we're doing out it is a real honor.
It was also pretty tough because I've got little kids.
So thinking about being gone away from them for eight months
was hard.
But knowing all the interesting stuff we're doing up here
makes it worthwhile.
Well, my good friend, your uncle, Juan Williams,
is imminently proud of you.
And he talks about how much this has been a source of joy
for your entire family and that you are making a sacrifice.
But I got to think with the holidays as well,
does that make it even more challenging with small children
to be a way knowing you're going to miss Christmas?
Yeah, I mean, it makes it hard.
But it also, in some ways, makes it easy.
I think one of the things that I've been so lucky with
is just seeing how much people come together
around something like this to help support each other.
And the amount of support that my wife and my kids
have from my family on the ground and from just my coworkers,
from everybody, our neighbors, is just overwhelming.
So I mean, I think it's hard to be away from my family
for the holidays, but also I get to spend some really awesome
holidays here with my space family, which
is really a pleasure.
So let's talk about where you are, the International Space
Station at a time when Washington
can't stop fighting over budgets and how to spend money
and where to spend it.
Why is the work that you're doing there important?
And how does it move us toward other space exploration,
whether it's back to the moon or eventually to Mars?
It's a great question.
I mean, the International Space Station
has been operating continuously for over 25 years
with people on it.
We actually just celebrated the 25th anniversary
earlier this while or at the beginning of November
of having this continuously inhabited.
And it's a special place because we can only,
it's a place that we can only do,
that there's some research that can only be done here,
research that involves microgravity.
And so this is helping us both on Earth with solving problems.
We've been working on things like developing drugs,
working on new ways of forming crystals
that you can really only do in microgravity.
But it's also helping us get further on.
This is a great test bed for a lot of the technologies
that we need for going to the moon with the Artemis program,
which we're embarking on right now, and also further on to Mars.
I'm up here for an eight month mission.
And that is, coincidentally, a similar time frame
that we think a flight out to Mars might take.
And so we're doing a lot of studies I'm involved in,
a lot of studies on how does being in space for the amount
of time affect the human body?
How do we keep ourselves healthy?
What does it do to us?
We're also doing a bunch of scientific experiments
looking at some of the technologies that are key
for getting out to Mars.
So things like life support systems.
How do we remove carbon dioxide from the air?
We have test demonstrators on the space station
for those technologies that we're going to be using on Mars
missions.
We're also looking at some things like how
to fluids behave in microgravity,
which is pretty important for transferring fluids
between two vehicles, which is something
that we're thinking of in our architecture for how
to get back to the moon.
So how do you prepare for a mission of this import
and this length?
I mean, physically, mentally, professionally?
What goes into getting ready?
Yeah, a lot goes into getting ready.
It's about a two year process from when
you get assigned to a mission to when you fly.
And you do a lot of technical training.
So learning all of the systems on the space station,
how to fix them, and also a lot of the science experiments
that you're going to be doing.
You learn one of the basics, one of the skills you need
to do the science experiments we know that we're going to do,
but also the ones that maybe haven't even been thought up yet.
But we'll try to execute during the eight months that I'm
up here.
We also do things like practice space walking
for any repairs or upgrades or experiments.
We might be doing outside the space station.
And then you also work on preparing your personal life,
your family, trying to get into a frame of mind
where you're building the support network and the community
that you need to be away for eight months,
but make sure that everybody's in good shape back at home.
So you do two years of preparation to go on this mission.
But I got to ask you now that you're actually there.
There's nothing else like that except being out there.
What does the world?
What's the universe look like from your approach at this point?
I got to say, one of the most incredible things
I've ever seen was the first time we have a module
on the space station called the Kupalo,
which basically has windows looking down at Earth.
It's almost kind of a full hemisphere that you can look out at.
And I would say that the first time that I got to look out
at that and see the Earth below me,
I mean, that was just absolutely breathtaking.
I've always been one of those people
that likes to sit in the window, see it on an airplane.
But this is just entirely next level.
I mean, just realizing that you're flying over continents,
it was absolutely breathtaking.
I think, you know, astronauts, I'd heard this before,
often say that you see the Earth as this fragile thing
and you don't see the borders of countries.
And, you know, it might sound a little bit trite,
but boy, that really does hit home
when you look at the Earth from up here,
just how fragile it is, but how just sort of one place it is as well.
Well, and the Space Station is a good illustration of that
because you're working with people from other countries
and ones that we may have some disputes with here back on Earth.
I mean, but there is an international framework
and cooperation for what you're doing there.
How important is that to the success of these missions?
It's absolutely essential.
I mean, this place would not work
without the cooperation of everybody involved.
I'm actually, well, I was gonna say standing,
but I'm actually floating here in the Japanese module,
the gem on our station, staring across,
that I'm staring across at the European module.
And I came up here on a spaceship
with two cosmonauts launched from Kazakhstan.
And, you know, every piece of the station
plays a really important role in allowing us
to carry out our mission.
And so, yeah, without cooperation,
we can't do all this amazing research.
And this research is really for the good of all,
for the good of all humanity.
And so, the fact that we can, you know,
have our disagreements on Earth,
but still collaborate here to work together
for the benefit of all, I think, is really, really powerful.
I'm curious, and I always wonder this,
how do you guys keep a schedule?
How do you sleep?
Do you walk on a 24-hour rotation?
I mean, just the logistics of what you're doing
and how you get rest and how you function
in a way that's so different, I would imagine.
Or maybe it's not, than here on Earth.
Yeah, it's actually not too different.
On the space station, we work on Greenwich Mean Time,
so, you know, same time zone as England.
And we wake up, we have actually a little scheduling app
that kind of has our tasks for the day,
but wake up at around, you know,
let's get to work, starting at around 7.30 in the morning.
We usually have some time built in.
It's pretty important for our bodies to exercise,
so we have a couple hours of exercise every day.
But basically, we have a schedule where our kind of day
is broken down into sort of 15-minute chunks
where we have tasks that we do, and then,
at the end of the day, we actually get a little bit of downtime
to call our families, to call home, read a book,
something like that, and go to sleep.
And one thing I'll say, you know,
having been up here for still less than a week, boy,
you sleep, at least I sleep, extremely comfortably up here.
It's like, well, you're floating.
It's like kind of floating in a bathtub.
It's been slept extremely well up here.
Well, I want to ask your advice as well,
because your uncle, Juan, wrote such a moving piece
in the Washington Post just about what this means to,
not only your family, but to our country, to the world,
the work that you're doing, the sacrifice that you're making.
But he talks about you being a little kid
in your onesie pajamas with rockets
and planes and outer space on them.
So this obviously is a dream.
You talked about working your whole life to get to this point.
What's your advice to a young person who has the same kinds
of dreams that you do about pushing these boundaries
and going to new places?
I really appreciate that question,
because it's something that I think is super important.
I mean, you know, for me, the path I took in life,
I was always fascinated by space and exploration.
And, you know, I think I'd realize,
by the time I was about 11 years old,
that actually being an astronaut wasn't, you know,
wasn't actually an attainable dream,
but the spark of the idea of space exploration
always stuck with me in it.
And it stuck with me to, and it inspired me
to pursue a lot of the things that I did.
I ended up studying physics and becoming an astronomer
and then working in medicine.
And, you know, nobody in my family before me
had ever done anything like this.
And it was only because I had that dream
and that spark and that excitement
and never really lost it that I sort of felt comfortable
enough to take these leaps and these jumps to say,
you know what, maybe I could actually get a PhD in physics.
Maybe that's something I could do.
Because I think, you know, there can be a lot of things
in the world that tell you there are things that you can't do,
but having that dream and that spark,
I think opens up doors that are there for you,
but you might not realize.
So I think that's something I think is really important
to take home is that when you dream
and when you have dreams,
it makes you realize you're full potential.
And I think that that was certainly, you know,
certainly the case for me.
I think, you know, I was very fortunate enough
to become an astronaut, but even the dream
of becoming an astronaut took me to a lot of places in life
I wouldn't have gotten to otherwise.
And I would have been extremely happy
and thrilled to get there regardless.
Obviously, I'm also extremely excited to be here,
but I think, you know, just following your dreams
takes you to a lot of really interesting places.
Now, wait until it's a little bit about your perspective

I wonder how it makes you feel in a bigger picture,

You know, I've heard other astronauts

Yeah, I think the smallness is definitely a big one.
I think, you know, realizing that when I look out the window

and care about and love is, well, there's a few people

And as part of the Artemis program,
as part of our Artemis II mission
to take humans back to the moon.
And I thought a lot about them in that moment
of seeing that about boy, you know,
I feel like I'm far away, they're going real far away.
Well, thank you for giving us some perspective,
taking time out of your mission there.
We are gonna stay in contact with what you were doing
over the months to come.
I know I speak for your uncle and so many others,
they're so proud of you, especially somebody from
this DMV area where I live and work and broadcast from
and just wish you the safest travels and study.
Well, you were there and I gotta say,
this is truly an out of this world interview in many ways.
So thank you Chris for your time, happy holidays.
It's really my pleasure and, you know,
give my regards to my uncle.
I was so glad he was able to come to mission control

and it was a really special experience.
And I'm really glad that, you know,
we were able to connect and talk.
This has been a fun experience.
You know, one of the joys of being up here

can give.
So I really appreciate you giving me the opportunity
to chat with you and your viewers.
It's, yeah, so thanks, thanks very much.
I appreciate it.
